Preface
Welcome to the CLES-FACIL Rocket Design technical manual.
This repository serves as an interactive reference and tutorial guide for rocket design, created for members of the CLES-FACIL association (cles-facil.org).

title: CLES-FACIL Rocket Design
text:
About This Manual
Our goal is to provide clear, interactive, and highly visual explanations of complex rocketry concepts, inspired by modern interactive textbooks. Whether you are a beginner looking to understand the basics of aerodynamics, or an advanced member working on structural optimization, you will find useful resources here.

Contents
Currently, this manual covers:

Fin Design & Stability: Understand fin geometry, the Barrowman equations, and compute your rocket’s stability margin through interactive calculators and visualizations.

More chapters on propulsion, recovery systems, and structures will be added soon.

title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Analysis
text:
1.1 Introduction
Fins are the primary means of ensuring passive aerodynamic stability on a rocket. When a rocket flies at a small angle of attack \(\alpha\) (i.e., it is slightly tilted relative to its velocity vector), aerodynamic forces act on its surfaces. Fins, placed at the rear of the rocket, generate a restoring moment that rotates the rocket back toward its flight path — much like the feathers on an arrow.
The key to understanding stability lies in two points:
The Barrowman equations (1966) provide an analytical method to compute the CP location for slender, finned rockets at small angles of attack. This chapter derives and implements them interactively.

title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Analysis
text:
Center of Gravity (CG): the point where the rocket’s mass is balanced. This is the pivot point around which the rocket rotates.
Center of Pressure (CP): the point where the resultant of all aerodynamic normal forces acts.







ImportantThe Stability Rule



For a rocket to be statically stable, the Center of Pressure must be located behind (aft of) the Center of Gravity. The distance between them, expressed in body diameters (calibers), is called the stability margin:
\[
\text{Stability Margin} = \frac{X_{CP} - X_{CG}}{d}
\]
A stability margin of 1.0 to 2.0 calibers is generally considered ideal for model rockets. Less than 1.0 caliber is marginally stable; less than 0.5 is unstable.

title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Analysis
1  Fin Design & Stability Analysis
text:
1.3 Barrowman Equations for Fins
The Barrowman method computes two quantities for each rocket component: the normal force coefficient derivative \(C_{N\alpha}\) and the center of pressure \(X_{CP}\). For a set of trapezoidal fins, the key equations are:

1.3.1 Fin Planform Area
\[
A_f = \frac{C_r + C_t}{2} \cdot s
\]


1.3.2 Mid-Chord Line Length
The mid-chord line connects the midpoints of the root and tip chords. Its length governs the effective sweep:
\[
\ell_{mc} = \sqrt{s^2 + \left(\ell_m + \frac{C_t - C_r}{2}\right)^2}
\]


1.3.3 Normal Force Coefficient Derivative
For a set of \(N\) fins on a body of diameter \(d\):
\[
(C_{N\alpha})_F = \frac{4\,N\,(s/d)^2}{1 + \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{2\,\ell_{mc}}{C_r + C_t}\right)^2}}
\]
This equation tells us how much restoring force the fins generate per radian of angle of attack. Higher values mean the fins are more effective at keeping the rocket aligned.


1.3.4 Fin-Body Interference Factor
The presence of the body tube accelerates airflow near the fin roots, increasing their effective lift. For 3 or 4 fins:
\[
K_{fb} = 1 + \frac{R}{s + R}
\]
where \(R = d/2\) is the body radius. The corrected coefficient is:
\[
(C_{N\alpha})_F^{\text{corrected}} = (C_{N\alpha})_F \cdot K_{fb}
\]


1.3.5 Fin Set Center of Pressure
The CP of the fin set, measured from the fin root leading edge:
\[
X_f = \frac{\ell_m\,(C_r + 2\,C_t)}{3\,(C_r + C_t)} + \frac{1}{6}\left(C_r + C_t - \frac{C_r\,C_t}{C_r + C_t}\right)
\]
To get the CP measured from the nose tip, add the distance from the nose tip to the fin root leading edge (\(X_{fLE}\)):
\[
X_{CP,\text{fins}} = X_{fLE} + X_f
\]

title: 1  Fin Design & Stability Analysis
text:
1.6 Assumptions & Limitations
The Barrowman method is valid under the following assumptions:

Small angle of attack — the rocket flies at \(\alpha < 10°\), where normal force varies linearly with \(\alpha\).
Subsonic, incompressible flow — Mach number \(Ma < 0.4\). No compressibility corrections are applied.
Slender, axisymmetric body — the rocket is long and thin relative to its diameter.
Sharp nose cone — blunt nose shapes may shift the CP forward from predicted values.
No body lift — the standard Barrowman method neglects lift generated by the body tube itself. Modified methods (Galejs, Rogers) account for this.
Rigid structure — no aeroelastic deformation of fins or body is considered.







TipFurther Reading




Barrowman, J.S. & Barrowman, J.A., “The Theoretical Prediction of the Center of Pressure”, 1966 — the original paper.
Nakka Rocketry — Barrowman Equations — excellent reference with worked examples.
RocketMime — Stability Calculator — another clear derivation.
